
Overview
Proximal humerus fractures are among the most common and challenging fractures
managed by orthopaedic surgeons. They occur in a bimodal distribution: high-energy
fractures occur in young males, and comminuted, osteoporotic, low-energy fractures
occur in elderly females.1 Treatment options vary and are based on the fracture pattern,
patient age, medical comorbidities, and functional demands.
Epidemiology
Frequency: 4% to 5% of all adult fractures (common)
Age and sex: bimodal distribution
High energy: younger men
Low energy: older women
Patterns may be similar based on the extent of osteoporosis

Epidemiology
Proximal humerus fractures are among the most common fractures encountered by
orthopaedic surgeons. They account for approximately 5% of all adult fractures and are
the third most common fracture in individuals older than 65 years.1 They occur in a
bimodal distribution with vastly different presentations and fracture patterns, and
various treatment options are available for young and older patients. High-energy
injuries typically occur in younger men, whereas low-energy, osteoporotic fractures are
observed in older women. In the elderly population, proximal humerus fractures occur
more frequently in females (3:1 ratio).2 These injuries tend to be highly comminuted and
difficult to manage because of underlying osteopenia and osteoporosis.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology

The proximal humerus consists of four parts: the humeral head, greater tuberosity, lesser
tuberosity, and diaphysis.
The head is separated from the diaphysis by the surgical neck (distal to the tuberosities) and
the anatomic neck (proximal to the tuberosities).
Fractures that extend into the surgical neck differ from those that involve the anatomic neck,
may require different surgical treatment options, and are associated with different insults to
the vascular supply.
The supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor muscles insert on the greater tuberosity.
The subscapularis muscle inserts on the lesser tuberosity.
Forces that deform the proximal humerus include the pectoralis major, which pulls the shaft
anterior and medial; the subscapularis, which internally rotates the lesser tuberosity and the
articular fragments; and the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor, which externally
rotate and/or pull the greater tuberosity proximally.

Osteology
To effectively and appropriately manage proximal humerus fractures, surgeons must
understand the complex anatomy of the shoulder girdle. The proximal humerus consists
of four parts (originally described by Codman)3: the humeral head, greater tuberosity,
lesser tuberosity, and humeral shaft. The articular portion of the humeral head is
separated from the greater and lesser tuberosities by the anatomic neck; the surgical
neck separates the humeral shaft from the greater and lesser tuberosities. The bicipital
groove contains the long head of the biceps tendon and separates the greater tuberosity
(lateral) and the lesser tuberosity (medial). The bicipital groove is used as a landmark
during reconstruction of the proximal humerus. These parts are important because of
the deforming muscular forces around the proximal humerus resulting in predictable
fracture patterns and displacement (Figure 1). Deforming forces around the shoulder
result from the pull of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, deltoid, and
pectoralis major tendons. The supraspinatus and infraspinatus attach to the greater
tuberosity and pull this fragment cranially and posteriorly, and the subscapularis
attaches to the lesser tuberosity and pulls medially. The deltoid translates the humeral
shaft cranially and the pectoralis major pulls the shaft anteriorly and medially.

Figure 1 Illustrations show the anatomy of the shoulder. A, The anatomy of the shoulder
is complex, and shoulder function depends on proper alignment and interaction of
anatomic structures. Displacement of fracture fragments is a result of the pull of
muscles attaching to the various bony components. The four anatomic components of
the proximal part of the humerus are the head (1), lesser tuberosity (2), greater
tuberosity (3), and shaft (4). The anatomic neck is at the junction of the head and
tuberosities, and the surgical neck is below the greater and lesser tuberosities
(metadiaphyseal junction). B, The subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity and
causes medial displacement, whereas the supraspinatus and infraspinatus insert on the
greater tuberosity and cause superior and posterior displacement. The pectoralis major
inserts on the humeral shaft and displaces it medially. (Panel A reproduced with
permission from Bohsali KI, Wirth MA: Fractures of the proximal humerus, in Rockwood
CA, Matsen FM III, Wirth MA, Lippitt SB, Fehringer EV, Sperling JW, eds: Rockwood and
Matsen’s The Shoulder, ed 5. Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2018, pp 183-242. Panel B adapted
with permission from Neer CS: Shoulder Reconstruction. Philadelphia, PA, WB Saunders,
1990, p 383.)
Vascular Anatomy
The axillary artery courses medial to the humerus and supplies the proximal humerus via the
anterior and posterior humeral circumflex arteries.
The anterior humeral circumflex branches into the arcuate artery of Liang, which runs in the
bicipital groove and terminates as a major blood supply to the greater tuberosity and the
humeral head (36%).

The posterior humeral circumflex artery is another major blood supply (64%) and traverses the
posterior head via the capsule, terminating in the greater tuberosity and the posterior
humeral head.
Fracture patterns that involve displacement of the tuberosities and neck may disrupt the
vascular supply of the humeral head and affect articular/head viability.
The vascular viability of the humeral head is likely preserved if 8 mm or more of the medial
calcar is intact with the head fragment.

Vascular Anatomy
The proximal humerus has a robust blood supply making osteonecrosis caused by an
arterial injury relatively uncommon in patients with a proximal humerus fracture4
(Figures 2 and 3). Blood is supplied to the proximal humerus via the anterior and
posterior humeral circumflex arteries, which branch from the third division of the
axillary artery.5
Figure 2 Illustration of a shoulder shows the proximal humeral vascularity: axillary
artery, anterior humeral circumflex artery, arcuate artery of Liang, and posterior
humeral circumflex artery. (Adapted from Jones CB, Eyberg BA: Proximal humerus
fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont,
IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 906-917.)

Figure 3 Image shows the microvasculature of the shoulder capsule and the labrum. The
inferior glenohumeral ligament complex has greater vascularity than the remainder of
the posterior capsule, which is relatively devoid of substantial vasculature. (Reproduced
with permission from O’Brien SJ, Carr JB II, Apostolakos J, Morse KW, Taylor SA:

Historically, the anterior humeral circumflex artery was thought to provide the dominant
circulation of the humeral head; however, it currently is thought that the posterior
humeral circumflex is the major blood supply.6 The posterior humeral circumflex
branches from the axillary artery and travels posteriorly with the axillary nerve through
the quadrilateral space and runs along the surgical neck to supply the posterior rotator
cuff and the posterior humeral head. The anterior humeral circumflex artery branches
from the axillary artery and runs along the inferior border of the subscapularis to the
bicipital groove. At this location, it branches into the arcuate artery, which travels parallel
to the long head of the biceps tendon in the bicipital groove and supplies the greater
tuberosity and the humeral head. The anterior and posterior humeral circumflex arteries
have an important anastomosis on the posterior rotator cuff that contributes to the vast
blood supply of the proximal humerus. If less than an 8-mm medial calcar hinge exists,
which is a surrogate for an intact posterior humeral circumflex artery, osteonecrosis of
the humeral head can be predicted.

Neural Anatomy
The axillary nerve courses from anterior to posterior in close proximity to the inferior glenoid
neck, anterior-inferior capsular pouch, and humeral neck; therefore, it is the most common
peripheral nerve injury.
Fracture-dislocations are associated with the highest risk of axillary nerve injury, which can
occur in 20% to 50% of all fracture-dislocations (based on electromyographic analysis). This
risk increases with glenohumeral dislocation and older age.

Neural Anatomy
The most commonly injured nervous structure in patients with a proximal humerus
fracture is the axillary nerve, particularly after fracture-dislocations, with an incidence of
20% to 50%. Mixed brachial plexopathies also are common.7 The axillary nerve arises
from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and travels with the posterior humeral
circumflex artery through the quadrilateral space. It then travels on the undersurface of
the deltoid muscle, approximately 6 cm distal to the lateral edge of acromion, and
innervates the teres minor and all heads of the deltoid.
Injury Classification
Based on the fracture pattern and predicts vascular viability, healing, and outcomes
Codman classification—Fracture lines occur along physeal scars; therefore, four segments
(head, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity, diaphysis).
Neer classification—Displaced is defined as 1 cm or greater and/or 45° of rotation; associated
with poor interobserver reliability.
Orthopaedic Trauma Association (OTA)/AO Foundation classification—Comprehensive long-
bone classification based on location, stability, comminution, and dislocation
Hertel binary (LEGO) classification—Five basic fracture locations resulting in 12 different
fracture patterns


Injury Classification
An effective classification system should be simple, be reproducible, and help determine
appropriate management and outcomes. Many classification systems are available for
proximal humerus fractures. The most commonly used classification system remains the
Neer classification, which is a modification of the original classification system described
by Codman in 1934.8 The Neer classification system is based on the parts of the
proximal humerus: humeral head, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity, and humeral
shaft. To be considered a true part, more than1 cm of displacement or more than 45°
degrees of angulation must be observed on any radiograph. Although improved with the
use of CT scans, the interobserver and intra-observer reliability of the Neer classification
system has consistently been poor; however, it remains the most widely used
classification system (Figure 4).

lesser tuberosity and the greater tuberosity. This results in six possible fractures with
two fragments, five possible fractures with three fragments, and one possible fracture
with four fragments (Figure 6).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A patient’s preinjury level of function, comorbidities, and expected level of compliance with
treatment must be determined. Patient and surgeon expectations also should be determined.
The mechanism of injury should be determined.
Low-energy injuries: The osseous quality should be evaluated.
High-energy injuries: Associated injuries, nerve function, and vascular integrity must be
evaluated.
Glenohumeral integrity (dislocation, labrum, rotator cuff).

Patient History
The clinical evaluation of a patient with a possible proximal humerus fracture begins
with a thorough patient history. To determine the appropriate treatment for specific
patients, a holistic view of the patient and their injury must be undertaken. Similar
fractures in two different individuals can be managed in two different manners and still
result in an acceptable outcome. The orthopaedic surgeon should have a thorough
understanding of the patient’s baseline functional status, preinjury shoulder conditions,
occupation, hobbies, handedness, medical comorbidities, and wishes before
determining management.
Proximal humerus fractures have a bimodal distribution, with high-energy fractures
occurring in young individuals and low-energy osteoporotic fractures occurring in elderly
individuals.1 A low-energy, ground-level fall is the most common cause of proximal
humerus fractures. High-energy injuries in young patients typically arise from a motor
vehicle collision or a fall from height. In either situation, surgeons must assess for

chest pain, neck pain, ipsilateral elbow or wrist pain, paresthesia, or weakness of the
involved extremity.
Physical Examination
The entire shoulder, neck, and thorax (pulmonary) are examined for associated injuries.

Physical Examination
For high- and low-energy injury mechanisms of injury, a thorough physical examination
should be performed with a focus on evaluating for associated injuries and with special
attention paid to the shoulder, neck, thorax, and ipsilateral elbow and wrist. Advanced
Trauma Life Support guidelines should be followed during the initial evaluation if
applicable. The patient likely will be guarding the involved extremity and be hesitant to
participate in a physical examination secondary to pain and apprehension. Assess for
ecchymosis, swelling, open wounds (which may be hidden in the axillary area), or
abrasions. Any open, bleeding wounds should increase suspicion for an open fracture.
Any gross deformity may be an indication of a fracture-dislocation. Gentle palpation
likely will yield pain and, perhaps, crepitus around the shoulder girdle. A strength and
range of motion (ROM) examination should be deferred for patient comfort.
Neurovascular Examination
A neurologic examination is performed as best as possible (pain often limits testing motor
function).

Neurovascular Examination
A thorough neurovascular examination is key and should include the entire brachial
plexus. The most likely injured nerve is the axillary nerve. Vascular status should be

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Injury radiographs (shoulder trauma series), including a true AP (Grashey), axillary (to ensure
head reduction but may falsely exaggerate fracture angulation), and scapular Y views, are
indicated for all fractures.

Radiography
Although patient discomfort occasionally makes radiographs difficult to obtain, all
patients in whom a proximal humerus fracture is suspected require true AP (Grashey),
axillary lateral, and scapular Y radiographs. These images are paramount and help guide
decision making. For most fractures, these three radiographic views may be all that is
necessary to make treatment decisions; however, surgeons must be careful in obtaining
these images because unnecessary movement of the arm may lead to pain and,
potentially, fracture displacement (Figure 7).

Computed Tomography
A CT scan with two-dimensional and three-dimensional reconstruction images may aid in
further evaluating the fracture pattern and may afford better visualization of head-split
fracture lines (marginal impaction, percentage of head involvement), fracture-dislocations,
glenoid lesions (determine approaches), and extensive comminution.

Computed Tomography
CT may provide valuable information to help guide treatment decisions if plain
radiographs are difficult to interpret (eg, with head-split fractures, fracture-dislocations,
associated glenoid fractures, and extensive comminution) (Figure 8).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI has limited indications, including associated dislocation (labrum, anterior capsule,
superior labrum anterior to posterior lesion, rotator cuff integrity).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely, MRI may be indicated in patients with an acute proximal humerus fracture. An
MRI provides useful information in assessing soft-tissue structures, such as the labrum,
capsule, and rotator cuff.12
Other Studies
CT angiography may be useful if concern for concomitant vascular injury exists.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Indications: minimal displacement, impacted displaced fractures, medical comorbidities,
osteoporosis, low functional demand, and low outcome expectations


Indications
Most low-energy proximal humerus fractures in elderly patients are minimally displaced
and can be successfully managed nonsurgically; however, the decision to proceed with
nonsurgical management is not made based on radiographs alone. The treating surgeon
must consider the entire patient, including premorbid function, handedness, occupation
and hobbies, functional demands, medical comorbidities, and patient wishes. A
substantially angulated, displaced fracture can be treated successfully without surgical
treatment in elderly patients with osteoporosis who have low functional
demands.11,13,14
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management is not simply benign neglect. Frequent follow-up examinations and
imaging studies are required. After pain has diminished, callus formation is present, and the
arm moves as a functional unit, self-directed or therapy-assisted exercises can begin. Starting
physical therapy too early or too late may be detrimental. Nonsurgical management often is
successful.
Nonsurgical management includes the use of a sling and rest until pain diminishes, followed
by a rotator cuff program, ROM activities. Activities of daily living (ADLs) are initiated until the
patient becomes skilled at a daily home program. Incorporating a sling and swathe (cuff and
collar) allows the deforming forces to relax and assists in aligning the fracture.

Techniques/Procedures
In deciding to manage a proximal humerus fracture nonsurgically, the patient must be
watched closely, especially during the first 1 to 3 weeks of treatment.12 Symptoms
should be managed via ice therapy, over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications,
and sleeping in a semi-erect position. Frequent follow-up, physical examination, and
imaging studies are required. The authors of this lesson recommend evaluating the
patient closely for the first 3 weeks via a physical examination and serial radiographs to
assess for any interval fracture displacement. Patients should be fitted with a sling or a

plateau at 1 year postinjury.
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications: young, high-demand patients, elderly patients with high expectations, cooperative
patients, displaced unstable nonimpacted fractures, fracture-dislocations, adequate bone
quality

Indications
Although most proximal humerus fractures can be successfully managed nonsurgically,
a subset of fractures necessitate surgical management to improve patient outcomes.
The decision to proceed with surgical treatment should be a joint decision between the
patient and physician. In offering surgical treatment to a patient with a proximal
humerus fracture, the surgeon should consider the fracture pattern and the patient’s
baseline functional status, medical comorbidities, occupation, and lifestyle.12 Typically,
surgical treatment is offered to young, high-demand patients and elderly patients with
high functional expectations. Surgical treatment also is indicated in appropriately
selected patients with a displaced, unstable fracture. Surgical treatment also is indicated
in patients with a fracture-dislocation.10 The goal of surgical management is a pain-free,
functional shoulder. This is most consistently achieved via anatomic reduction and

Techniques/Procedures
Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
Limited indications: for simple fracture patterns, compliant patients, experienced surgeons;
primarily used om the pediatric population.
Contraindications—Should not be used for the management of dislocations (need for early
ROM), metaphyseal comminution/diaphyseal extension (problems achieving a stable anchor
point), severe osteoporosis (relative), or head-split fracture (unable to achieve early ROM and
stable fixation).
Pins are inserted initially under power and then advanced by hand terminally to avoid head
penetration; two to four pins are placed lateral to proximal and two greater tuberosity pins
(90-90 fixation) are inserted divergently and cut under the skin to avoid infection.
Pins are removed in the office or surgical suite at 6 weeks postoperatively; unlimited ROM
and strengthening are then initiated.
Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
Indications: all types of fractures, including head-split, diaphyseal extension, and
comminution
Contraindications—Unreconstructible fracture patterns; fracture-dislocation may be a
relative contraindication to ORIF in elderly patients because one-half of these patients may
undergo revision surgery for failure.
Implants
Limited fixation—Combination of pin, cannulated screw, suture, and tension band wiring;
best reserved for isolated tuberosity fractures and impacted (not comminuted) fractures.
Nonlocking implants—Reserved for good quality bone
Locked plating implants—Used in compromised bone, comminution, and short-segment
fixation. This has become the most common implant of choice for proximal humerus fixation
based on the poor track record of other fixation methods; however, technical failures are still
common.
Approaches
Deltopectoral—Preferred approach, most common; can fix or replace via this approach; may
be problematic with displaced greater tuberosity fractures or fractures with considerable

Extended anterolateral acromial, deltoid splitting—Increased risk to axillary nerve (6 cm distal

Reduction techniques
Soft-tissue integrity should be maintained, especially medially along the calcar.
Rotator cuff attachments are used for tuberosity mobilization and stabilization with sutures.
Joystick mobilization of the head, tuberosity, and shaft with the use of provisional 2.5-mm
Schantz pins; also an aid for reduction as a unit for fracture-dislocations.
With comminution and limited calcar stability, a fibular strut graft or other endosteal
substitution may be helpful.
Plate application
Lateral to the bicipital groove to enhance symmetrical screw insertion and diminish head
penetration
Distal to the rotator cuff insertion to avoid subacromial impingement and enhance calcar
screw (kickstand screw) insertion
Usually involves elevation of the deltoid insertion
Intramedullary nailing (IMN)

Rehabilitation
Nonsurgical management begins with a period of rest in a sling. Pendulum exercises can
begin within the first 2 weeks to prevent stiffness. A sling is used for 4 to 6 weeks and
can be discontinued after pain at rest has resolved and fracture callous is visible on
radiographs. Passive and active ROM can begin at approximately 6 weeks via a self-
directed or therapist-guided program. ADLs also can be initiated around the 6-week
mark. After active and passive ROM have been restored to normal, a supervised
strengthening program can begin. Because of the complexity of the shoulder girdle, the
authors of this lesson routinely advise patients that it may take as long as 5 months to
reach 90% improvement and 1 year to reach maximum recovery.
Similar to the rehabilitation program for nonsurgical management, the authors of this
lesson prefer a slow and steady progression. After surgical fixation, the selected
construct should be able to withstand passive ROM immediately postoperatively. A sling
is used for pain control for the first 2 to 4 weeks postoperatively. If the rotator cuff was
repaired during fixation or arthroplasty, active motion should not be initiated before 6
weeks postoperatively. A gradual active motion program can then begin and should be
transitioned to a strengthening program after full motion has returned. This may be self-
directed or under the direction of a certified physical therapist. Similarly, 1 year may be
required before attaining maximal improvement.

Outcomes
Outcomes after a proximal humerus fracture may be quite variable.31,32,36,37 Room for
improvement exists in the surgical management of these injuries. The most important
factor is selecting the appropriate treatment option for the appropriate patient. A
severely comminuted, displaced four-part fracture may be best managed nonsurgically
in elderly patients with low functional demands. The best outcome in such patients is a
painless shoulder.
Appropriate expectations should be provided to patients with these injuries. With
nonsurgical or surgical management, improvement can be expected for up to 1 year
postinjury. Similar to most injuries managed by orthopaedic surgeons, the best
outcomes occur in motivated, compliant patients.
